newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Foreign carmakers eye Russia, local firms struggle.
newsitem.headline: Foreign carmakers eye Russia, local firms struggle.

text.p: Foreign automakers see growing opportunities to build and sell cars in the former Soviet Union, but most vehicle manufacturers from the region have problems, speakers at a conference in Moscow said on Wednesday.
"The Russian market offers a lot of growth potential in the medium-to-long term," said Wolfgang Vollath, director of Russia for German automaker Bayerische Motoren Werke AG (BMW).
But analysts and officials said domestic car makers, struggling to throw off a reputation for poor quality, could find it hard to capitalise on the opportunity.
"Russian cars and trucks are obsolete and they don't meet customer requirements," said Deputy Russian Transport Minister Viktor Berezin. "Drastic modernisation is needed."
Car sales doubled in Russia from 1985 to 1995, but demand remains high -- analysts say there are under 80 cars per 1,000 residents in Russia, compared to 560 in the United States.
"Russia's market for new cars could be as high as 1.5 million units a year, but domestic manufacturers built only 822,000 cars in 1995," Vollath said.
The market has already developed a western-style pecking order as prosperous Russians flaunt their wealth by buying expensive cars, Vollath said.
"The demand for luxury cars is increasing in Russia," he said. "There is enough money to back this demand, although the macroeconomic indications in Russia are still disappointing."
Vollath said BMW was looking to assemble cars in Russia to exploit demand and avoid punitive taxes on imported vehicles.
The German carmaker would be the first company to build premium cars in the former Soviet Union, apart from the austere and tank-like ZiL limousines used by top government officials.

But the region's biggest planned investment is a project of up to $1 billion involving Korean automaker Kia Motors Corp. Kia plans to ship kits of its cars and commercial vehicles for assembly in Kaliningrad, a Russian enclave on the Baltic Sea. Output could be at least 100,000 units at capacity.
Foreign automakers also plan to build cars in Russia and compete in segments already served by local carmakers.
The Niva, a basic off-road vehicle from Russia's largest automaker AO AvtoVAZ, will be upstaged when U.S. General Motors Corp starts assembling Chevrolet Blazers.

GM said assembly would start in December in a joint venture with Elabuga Avtomobilny Zavod ElAZ, an enterprise majority owned by the government of the autonomous region of Tartarstan, some 1,400 kilometers east of Moscow.
The Blazer will boost supply of sport-utility vehicles here. Demand is great in other market segments as well, and observers say local manufacturers are increasingly unable to satisfy it.

The problem has affected Ukraine as well, and Yuri Yakovenko, auto industry director for Ukraine's Ministry of Machine Building and Conversion said domestic firms built only four of the 13 types of vehicles in demand.
"We can meet only 20 percent of demand for trucks and 30 percent of demand for cars," Yakovenko said. "We lack light trucks, mid-sized trucks and heavy trucks."
The only automaker in the former Soviet Union that has been aggressively modernising is AO Gorkovsky Avtomobilny Zavod (GAZ) Russia's second-biggest automaker.
GAZ is saddled with old products, but it pioneered light- commercial vehicles in Russia in the mid-1990s with its Gazelle models, the top-selling brand in the former Soviet Union.

GAZ outlined sweeping plans to build new cars and trucks at the conference. This undertaking might be overly ambitious, and the sources of finance for the new products are not clear, but analysts said GAZ has what it takes to succeed.

"Management seems to have the right focus -- do the basics right," said Dagmar Bottenbruch, research director of MC Securities in London. "GAZ is actively seeking to improve its distribution, supplies of spare parts and product quality. GAZ looks like a survivor." -- Moscow newsroom +7 095 941 8520
